exercises.attribution: Original prose written for the LIFT knowledge base (CC BY 4.0).
commonMistakes: Walking so slowly it barely raises the heart rate
Going so hard it becomes a run and can't be sustained
Slouching with the head down at the phone
cues: Brisk enough that talking takes effort, but you still can
Tall posture, arms swinging naturally
Nose breathing if possible — a rough zone 2 gauge
instructions: Warm up with 3-5 minutes of easy walking.
Pick up the pace to brisk: you should feel your heart rate rise and your breathing deepen, but still be able to speak in full sentences.
Maintain that pace for the target duration — 20 to 45 minutes is the sweet spot for a zone 2 session.
Cool down with 3-5 minutes of easy walking. Note your duration; distance and route are secondary.
exercises.longevityNotes: If one habit predicted healthy aging, it would be this: regular moderate cardio. Zone 2 work builds the mitochondrial base that powers everything — heart health, metabolic health, brain health — and brisk walking is the most accessible dose. No gym, no gear, no recovery cost. The research is unambiguous: 150+ minutes a week of this transforms risk profiles. It is the highest-return movement in this entire library.
exercises.name: Brisk Walk

progression.loadingGuidance: Add 5 minutes per session each week until you reach 45 minutes, then add a second weekly session before increasing intensity.
progression.regressTo: Easy walk, any duration — consistency beats intensity

exercises.safetyNotes: If you have a cardiac condition, clear moderate cardio with your clinician first. In heat, carry water and shorten the session; in winter, watch for ice.

sources.title: ACSM Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription

exercises.attribution: Original prose written for the LIFT knowledge base (CC BY 4.0).
commonMistakes: Letting the lower back arch off the floor
Holding your breath instead of breathing behind the brace
Moving the arms and legs too fast to feel the core working
cues: Press your lower back into the floor like you're squashing a grape
Exhale as the opposite arm and leg extend
Slow is the point — if it's easy, you're going too fast
instructions: Lie on your back with arms extended toward the ceiling and hips and knees bent to 90 degrees. Press your lower back flat into the floor.
Brace your core and slowly extend your right arm overhead while straightening your left leg, hovering both just above the floor.
Pause, then return to the start position with control. Your lower back must not arch at any point.
Repeat on the opposite side. That is one rep per side; alternate for the full set.
exercises.longevityNotes: The dead bug trains the deep core the way your spine actually needs it — resisting extension under load, which is what protects your back when you lift, carry, and twist in real life. Unlike sit-ups, it builds stability without grinding the lumbar spine through repeated flexion. A quiet, braced trunk is the foundation every other lift in this library stands on.
exercises.name: Dead Bug

progression.loadingGuidance: When you can do 3 sets of 10 per side with zero back arch, slow the tempo to 4 seconds per rep or add a light band.
progression.regressTo: Supine 90-90 breathing with a light brace (no limb movement)

exercises.safetyNotes: If you feel your lower back lifting off the floor, shorten the range — only extend as far as you can keep the back pinned down. Skip if you have an acute abdominal strain.

sources.title: Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning

exercises.attribution: Original prose written for the LIFT knowledge base (CC BY 4.0).
commonMistakes: Shrugging the shoulders up to the ears
Holding your breath
Swinging the body
cues: Shoulders down, away from ears
Relaxed jaw, steady breathing
Full grip, thumb wrapped
instructions: Grip an overhead bar with both hands, palms facing away, hands just outside shoulder-width.
Step off the support and let your body hang with straight arms, feet off the ground.
Keep your shoulders pulled slightly down away from your ears — don't shrug up.
Breathe calmly and hang for time. Step back onto the support to finish.
exercises.longevityNotes: Grip strength is one of the most-studied correlates of healthy aging, and the dead hang builds it alongside shoulder health and spinal decompression. It's also zero-impact and self-limiting — you simply let go when you're done. Accumulate 2-3 minutes of total hang time per week; it doubles as a daily shoulder-health habit.
exercises.name: Dead Hang

progression.loadingGuidance: Add 5-10 seconds per set when you can finish all sets without grip failure.
progression.regressTo: Feet-supported hang (toes on a box, partial bodyweight)

exercises.safetyNotes: Skip or modify if you have an acute shoulder injury or uncontrolled high blood pressure. Stop if you feel sharp shoulder pain rather than muscular fatigue.

sources.title: ACSM Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription

exercises.attribution: Original prose written for the LIFT knowledge base (CC BY 4.0).
commonMistakes: Leaning away from the weights or shrugging excessively
Shuffling with tiny rushed steps instead of controlled strides
Holding your breath for the whole carry
cues: Tall chest, ribs down
Crush the handles
Walk like you're balancing a book on your head
instructions: Pick up a heavy dumbbell or kettlebell in each hand and stand tall.
Pull your shoulders slightly back and down, brace your core as if for a light punch.
Walk with short, controlled steps, keeping your torso upright — no leaning or swaying.
Set the weights down with control by hinging at the hips. Rest, then repeat.
exercises.longevityNotes: Carrying heavy things is a fundamental human movement — groceries, luggage, grandchildren. The farmer carry trains grip, posture, and core stability all at once, and it's self-regulating: your grip gives out long before anything dangerous happens. Walk 30-60 seconds per set, 2-3 times a week; your future self carrying groceries will thank you.
exercises.name: Farmer Carry

progression.loadingGuidance: Increase weight when you can carry for 60 seconds with perfect posture at RPE 7 or less.
progression.progressTo: Trap-bar carry or heavier dumbbells for distance
progression.regressTo: Single-arm suitcase carry with a light weight

exercises.safetyNotes: Clear your walking path first. If you have lower-back issues, start light and keep carries short; stop if you feel the need to lean sideways to compensate.

sources.title: ACSM Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription

exercises.attribution: Original prose written for the LIFT knowledge base (CC BY 4.0).
commonMistakes: Heels lifting off the floor
Lower back rounding at the bottom of the rep
Knees caving inward on the way up
cues: Chest tall, weight close
Knees track over toes
Whole foot pressed into the floor
instructions: Hold a dumbbell or kettlebell vertically at chest height, elbows tucked under the weight.
Stand with feet slightly wider than shoulder-width, toes turned out 15-30 degrees.
Push your hips back and bend your knees, keeping your chest tall and the weight close to your body.
Descend until your elbows touch the insides of your knees, or as deep as you can without your lower back rounding.
Drive through your whole foot to stand, squeezing your glutes at the top.
exercises.longevityNotes: The squat pattern is how you sit, stand, and get off the floor for the rest of your life — train it for depth and control, not maximal load. A deep, easy goblet squat you can still do at 80 beats a heavy barbell you abandon at 50. Keep 2-3 reps in reserve; joint-friendly volume beats grinding singles for healthspan.
exercises.name: Goblet Squat

progression.loadingGuidance: Add 2-4 kg when you can complete 3 sets of 12 with clean form at RPE 7 or less.
progression.regressTo: Bodyweight box squat to a chair or bench

exercises.safetyNotes: If you have a knee replacement or acute knee pain, limit depth to your pain-free range and check with your clinician first. Never bounce out of the bottom position.

sources.title: ACSM Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription

exercises.attribution: Original prose written for the LIFT knowledge base (CC BY 4.0).
commonMistakes: Hips sagging so the body bends at the waist
Shrugging the shoulders up toward the ears
Using momentum instead of a controlled pull
cues: Pull your chest to the bar, elbows driving back
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top
Keep your body rigid — no sagging, no piking
instructions: Set a bar (or suspension-trainer handles) at about waist height. Lie underneath it and grip the bar with hands slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Walk your feet forward until your body hangs in a straight line, heels on the floor. The steeper your body angle, the harder the rep.
Pull your chest to the bar, driving your elbows back and squeezing your shoulder blades together.
Lower under control to straight arms. Keep your glutes braced so your body stays a rigid plank throughout.
exercises.longevityNotes: Pulling strength balances all the pushing and sitting of modern life, and it's the foundation of a healthy upper back and posture. The inverted row is the most joint-friendly way to build it — your feet stay on the ground, so you can scale the difficulty precisely and train the pulling pattern for decades without beating up your shoulders. Strong lats and rhomboids are what keep you upright at 80.
exercises.name: Inverted Row

progression.loadingGuidance: Lower the bar (steeper body angle) when you can do 3 sets of 12 with a 1-second pause at the top.
progression.regressTo: Standing band row at chest height

exercises.safetyNotes: Make sure the bar or anchor is secure before loading your full body weight. If you have an acute shoulder injury, keep the range pain-free and avoid the bottom stretch position.

sources.title: Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning

exercises.attribution: Original prose written for the LIFT knowledge base (CC BY 4.0).
commonMistakes: Arching the lower back to heave the weight up
Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears at the top
Pressing the weights out in front instead of overhead
cues: Ribs down, glutes squeezed — no lean-back
Press up and slightly in, biceps finishing by your ears
Lower with control to the starting position every rep
instructions: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding dumbbells at shoulder height, palms facing each other or slightly forward. Brace your core and squeeze your glutes.
Press the weights overhead until your arms are fully extended, biceps finishing roughly by your ears. Do not lean back.
Pause briefly at the top without shrugging your shoulders.
Lower the weights back to shoulder height with control. That is one rep.
exercises.longevityNotes: Overhead strength is independence: putting luggage in the bin, reaching the top shelf, catching yourself in a fall. The standing press builds it while forcing the core and glutes to stabilize — a full-body investment from one movement. Keep the loads moderate and the reps clean; cranky shoulders come from grinding heavy singles, not from patient sub-maximal volume.
exercises.name: Overhead Press

progression.loadingGuidance: Add the smallest available increment when you can complete 3 sets of 10 with no back arch at RPE 7 or less.

exercises.safetyNotes: If you have shoulder impingement, keep the reps pain-free and stop well short of lockout if the top position pinches. Never press behind the neck.

sources.title: Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning

exercises.attribution: Original prose written for the LIFT knowledge base (CC BY 4.0).
commonMistakes: Hips sagging below the body line
Flaring the elbows out to 90 degrees
Only lowering halfway and calling it a rep
cues: Body straight as a plank from head to heels
Elbows at roughly 45 degrees from your torso
Chest to the floor, or as close as your strength allows
instructions: Start in a high plank: hands under shoulders, body in a straight line from head to heels, glutes and core braced.
Lower your chest toward the floor by bending your elbows, keeping them about 45 degrees from your torso.
Descend until your chest nearly touches the floor, or as deep as you can while keeping your hips level.
Push the floor away to return to the start, fully extending your arms without shrugging your shoulders.
exercises.longevityNotes: Push-up capacity is one of the simplest field tests of upper-body health — studies link higher push-up counts with lower cardiovascular event risk in men. Beyond the numbers, it's the movement of getting yourself off the floor, and it trains the chest, shoulders, and triceps with zero equipment for life. Full range beats half reps; elevate your hands to keep every rep honest.
exercises.name: Push-Up

progression.loadingGuidance: When you can do 3 sets of 15 clean reps, progress to feet-elevated push-ups or add a weighted vest.
progression.regressTo: Incline push-up with hands on a bench or wall

exercises.safetyNotes: If you have a shoulder impingement or recent rotator-cuff issue, keep reps pain-free and reduce range before adding volume. Stop if you feel pinching at the front of the shoulder.

sources.title: ACSM Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription

exercises.attribution: Original prose written for the LIFT knowledge base (CC BY 4.0).
commonMistakes: Rounding the lower back to reach further down
Bending the knees into a squat instead of hinging at the hips
Letting the weight drift away from the legs
cues: Push your hips straight back, like closing a car door behind you
Weight slides down your thighs, close to your body
Feel a deep stretch in the hamstrings, then squeeze the glutes to stand
instructions: Stand tall holding the weight in front of your thighs, feet hip-width apart, knees softly bent.
Brace your core and push your hips straight back, letting the weight slide down the fronts of your thighs.
Keep your back flat and your chest proud as you lower until you feel a deep stretch in your hamstrings, usually just below the knees.
Drive your hips forward and squeeze your glutes to return to standing. Do not hyperextend your lower back at the top.
exercises.longevityNotes: The hip hinge is the movement you use every time you pick something off the floor — groceries, grandchildren, a dropped pen. Training it keeps the posterior chain (glutes, hamstrings, spinal erectors) strong and teaches a spine-safe lifting pattern that protects your back for decades. Load it progressively but never maximally; a crisp, controlled hinge at RPE 7 beats a sloppy max that costs you a disc.
exercises.name: Romanian Deadlift

progression.loadingGuidance: Add 2-5 kg when you can complete 3 sets of 10 with a flat back and full hamstring stretch at RPE 7 or less.
progression.progressTo: Barbell Romanian deadlift from a deficit
progression.regressTo: Dowel hip-hinge drill (no weight, dowel along the spine)

exercises.safetyNotes: If you have an acute disc issue or radiating leg pain, skip loaded hinging until cleared by your clinician. Stop the set the moment your lower back starts to round — depth is earned, not forced.

sources.title: Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning

exercises.attribution: Original prose written for the LIFT knowledge base (CC BY 4.0).
commonMistakes: Front knee collapsing inward
Torso leaning far forward over the front thigh
Pushing off the back foot instead of driving through the front leg
cues: Tall torso, ribs stacked over hips
Front knee tracks over the middle of your foot
Drive through the whole front foot to stand
instructions: Take a long staggered stance, one foot forward and one back, torso tall and core braced. Hold onto a wall or rack for balance if needed.
Lower straight down until your front thigh is roughly parallel to the floor and your back knee hovers just above the ground.
Keep most of your weight on the front leg; the back leg is a kickstand, not a driver.
Drive through your front foot to stand. Complete all reps on one side before switching.
exercises.longevityNotes: Single-leg strength is balance, and balance is independence: falls are the leading cause of injury in older adults, and the split squat trains the exact pattern — one leg loaded, body stable — that keeps you on your feet. It also evens out left-right strength differences that bilateral squats hide. Start bodyweight, hold a wall, and earn your depth; the goal is a controlled single-leg squat you can still do at 75, not a wobbly weighted one today.
exercises.name: Split Squat

progression.loadingGuidance: Add dumbbells when you can do 3 sets of 10 per leg with a 2-second pause at the bottom, no balance assist.
progression.regressTo: Assisted split squat holding a doorframe or TRX

exercises.safetyNotes: If you have acute knee pain, shorten the range to your pain-free zone and keep the front knee behind the toes initially. Use balance support freely — a fall during the exercise defeats its purpose.

programs.attribution: Original programming written for the LIFT knowledge base (CC BY 4.0).
programs.goal: Build the fundamental movement patterns (squat, carry, hang) with joint-friendly volume over 4 weeks. Designed for beginners or returning lifters; every session caps at RPE 8.
programs.name: Longevity Foundations

blocks.notes: Week 1: start at the low end of the rep range.
Choose a weight you can carry with perfect posture.
Accumulate hang time; step down before grip fully fails.
Add one set vs Day 1. Same weight unless all sets felt RPE 6 or less.
Easy day: stop each set with 1-2 seconds in reserve.
